title: The role of the dorsal stream during speech perception in cochlear implant users
summary:
People with cochlear implants (CI) cope with everyday life in very different ways. Some understand speech well with their CI, while others have more difficulty, especially when the environment is noisy or many people are talking at once. There can be various reasons for this. We want to find out why this is the case. To do this, we are using a new method to look at what happens in the brain when people hear speech. We want to compare the results from the new method with results from a commonly used method. In addition, we are comparing the results of the new method between CI users and people with normal hearing on the one hand, and between CI users with good speech comprehension and those with poorer speech comprehension on the other. 

Our research questions are:
How do the activities in the brain differ between the two measurement methods? Are the same regions of the brain activated in subjects with CI as in subjects with healthy hearing?
And is there a difference between people who understand speech well in noisy environments and those who have more difficulty doing so?

In the study, we would like to use two methods that allow us to measure blood flow in the brain from the outside. In the new method, we will attach sensors to the head using a head cap (similar to a swimming cap) to measure blood flow. We will also use additional sensors to record physiological processes (heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, body temperature, and respiration). For the second method, you will participate in an MRI scan. Both methods are non-invasive, meaning they are painless and do not require anything to be inserted into the body. We want to find out how the brain reacts to speech with and without background noise. We also measure the size of the pupils and observe eye movements. This can show us how strenuous it was for you to understand speech in noisy or quiet environments.
conditions: Mixed conductive and sensorineural hearing loss, bilateral

interventions.name: Control group of normal hearing participants: fNIRS / fMRT measurements during speech perception with noise
Experienced cochlear-implant users: fNIRS / fMRT measurements during speech perception in noise
Newly implanted cochlear-implant users: fNIRS measurements during speech perception in noise at different timepoints during rehabilitation phase

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Normal hearing for his age
- CI candidate
- Experienced CI user
- Native language: German
- Right-handed
Exclusion criteria:
- neurological disorders
- cognitive impairments
- left-handed
- hearing loss (not age-related)
- not suitable for MRI
